extracted.intended_audience: poets and writers interested in composing epistolary verse; readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing epistolary (letter-form) poetry in two classical modes (Ovidian and Horatian), including stylistic qualifications, subject handling, and editorial remarks about publication and correspondence. Targeted at poets aiming to write letters in verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Epistolary Poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary Poetry may be reduced into two classes: (1) Love-Letters, Letters of Friendship, and Letters upon mournful Occasions (the Ovidian way); (2) Familiar, Critical, and Moral Epistles, with Letters of Mirth and Humour (the Horatian way).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ovid is the exemplar for the first class; Horace for the latter. The author limits discussion to those types in use among the Ancients and copied by some Moderns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for the Ovidian way
rubrics_metrics.description: He that is ambitious of succeeding in the Ovidian way, should first examine his Heart well, and feel whether his Passions (especially those of the gentler Kind) play easie, since it is not his Wit, but the Delicacy and Tenderness of his Sentiments, that will affect his Readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versification should be soft, with numbers flowing and querulous; success depends on delicacy and tenderness of sentiment rather than mere wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for the Horatian epistolary style
rubrics_metrics.description: The Qualifications requisite for writing Epistles, after the Model given us by Horace, are of a quite different Nature: He that would excel must have a good Fund of strong Masculine Sense; a thorough Knowledge of Mankind; an Insight into the Business, and the prevailing Humours of the Age; a Mind well seasoned with the finest Precepts of Morality; and be filled with nice Reflections upon the bright and the dark sides of human Life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional requirements: be a master of refined raillery; understand delicacies and absurdities of conversation; have a lively turn of wit; use an easy and concise manner of expression; write in a free and disengaged manner; avoid appearing a recluse; draw illustrations, comparisons, and images from common life; judiciously throw in strokes of satire, criticism, and panegyric as by the by; but always 'remember that he writes in Verse' and take more than ordinary care not to fall into prose or vulgar diction. (Note: Horace himself is sometimes thought careless about versification.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating sublime subjects in the epistolary way
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects of the most sublime Nature are often treated in the Epistolary way with advantage, as in Horace's epistle to Augustus: the poet surprises us with pomp and seems rather betrayed into his Subject than to have aimed at it by Design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the dignity of the subject hurries the poet into descriptions and sentiments, it is usual for him to recollect himself and fall back gracefully into the natural style of a letter. The effect can be like a visit of a king incognito: a mixture of familiarity and grandeur. Example: a recent epistolary poem on the King's accession is noted as happily observing this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding excessive obscurity in riddling lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Translated poem is noted as 'Every Line in it is a Riddle, and the Reader must be forced to consider it twice or thrice' before understanding images (e.g., the Cynick's Tenement is a Tub, Bacchus his Cast-coat a Hogs-head).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit guidance: excessive obscurity requiring multiple re-readings may be a stylistic choice (riddle-like), but authors should be aware this demands more effort from readers and can obscure meaning; weigh cleverness of riddle against reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial handling of reader correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor records many incoming letters and offers brief dispositions: refer certain queries to specialists (e.g., 'Referred to the Dumb Man for an Answer'); decline to publish some letters; postpone others; return manuscripts; preserve originals for posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical editorial rules illustrated: (a) route technical or conscience-cases to appropriate authorities (minister, society, censor); (b) refuse to print material at author's request or on other grounds; (c) preserve original letters in a dedicated room for possible future publication; (d) use brief, sometimes wittily-worded replies or public annotations to explain disposition (e.g., 'Rejected', 'Postponed', 'Not to be printed entire').
